transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I’m Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what’s been troubling you and what brings you in today?

Yeah… I guess the thing that finally pushed me to actually call the employee assistance program was my sleep. It sounds kind of basic, but I’m just not sleeping right at all. I’ll go to bed tired, but then I lie there with my mind going over work stuff, conversations I had, things I should’ve said differently… and then arguments at home too. It’s like I can’t get my brain to shut off.

And even when I do fall asleep, I’m waking up at like 3 or 4 in the morning, just wide awake, and then the day starts before it even starts, if that makes sense. I get up feeling like I never really rested. It’s been wearing me down enough that I figured I should talk to someone instead of just trying to push through it.
When you're having trouble sleeping, is it mostly that you can't fall asleep at the beginning of the night, or that you wake up very early and can't go back to sleep?

It’s kind of both, honestly. At the start of the night I’ll get into bed feeling exhausted, like I should just be able to pass out, but then my head starts running through everything—work stuff, conversations from the day, things I maybe handled wrong, and then sometimes arguments at home too. So I can lie there for a while just… not able to shut it off.

And then even if I do eventually fall asleep, I’m waking up around 3 or 4 in the morning, like fully awake, and I can’t really get back into a decent sleep after that. So by the time I actually get up, it feels like I never really rested in the first place. That’s honestly what pushed me to call the employee assistance program—I just felt like I wasn’t sleeping right at all and it was catching up with me.

Do you find that you worry a lot during the day, even when you're not trying to sleep? Like, does your mind often jump to things you’re anxious about, even when you’d rather not be thinking about them?

I’m not totally sure how to separate it, honestly. During the day, I mean… I do have things on my mind, but I don’t know if I’d call it worrying all day in the way you mean. Like, I’m not sitting there thinking, “I’m anxious, I’m anxious,” the whole time.

It’s more that when there’s a quiet moment, my brain will kind of drift back to stuff I probably don’t need to be replaying. Work things, mostly, or little interactions where I wonder if I handled something badly. But during the day I can usually keep moving because there’s something to do, or someone needs something from me, so I don’t notice it as much. It gets louder at night, if that makes sense.

So… yes and no? I don’t know if that answers it. I guess I haven’t really paid attention to whether it’s constant during the day. I’ve mostly noticed it because it gets in the way when I’m trying to sleep.
Do you find yourself feeling very tired or lacking energy during the day because of how poorly you've been sleeping at night?

Yeah, definitely. I mean, I don’t know if it’s purely from the sleep or just the whole cycle of it, but I feel like I’m starting the day already behind. I wake up around 3 or 4 and I’m just… up, or half-up, and then when the alarm finally comes it doesn’t feel like I’ve actually rested.

So during the day I’m dragging more than I used to. It’s not like I’m collapsing or anything, but I feel worn down, like I’m running on a low battery. And that’s really what made me call the employee assistance program in the first place — I kept thinking, “Okay, I can push through one rough night,” but it’s been this pattern of lying there replaying work stuff or arguments at home, then waking up early, and then trying to function the next day like I slept normally. It just catches up with you.
Do you find yourself feeling anxious or on edge most days, even when there isn't a specific problem happening at that moment?

I’m not sure I’d say “most days,” at least not in a clear way. I know that probably sounds like I’m splitting hairs, but I don’t walk around constantly feeling on edge for no reason, like I’m bracing for something all day long.

There are moments where I feel keyed up, I guess, but usually I can connect it to something—work, something I need to handle, something I’m replaying in my head. If there’s nothing specific happening, I don’t always notice anxiety as the main thing. It’s more like I’m… tense sometimes, or preoccupied, but I don’t know if I’d call it being anxious most of the day.

Honestly, I think I notice it more when things get quiet and I’m left with my thoughts. During the day I’m usually busy enough that I can push through or distract myself. So I’m not sure I have a clean yes or no. I guess I haven’t really been tracking it that closely.
Over the past couple of weeks, have you found yourself feeling fatigued or lacking energy most days, even when you haven’t been particularly busy or physically active?

I’m honestly not sure how to answer that cleanly. I mean, I have felt tired, yes, but when you say “most days” and “even when I haven’t been busy,” I kind of get stuck, because my days usually feel mentally full even if I’m not doing anything physically demanding.

Like, I don’t have a job where I’m lifting boxes or running around all day, but I still end up feeling drained by the end of it, and sometimes even earlier than that. But I can’t tell if that counts as fatigue in the way you mean, or if it’s just normal being worn out from work and life and not resting well. I haven’t really been tracking it day by day.

There are definitely days where I think, “Why am I this tired? I haven’t even done that much,” but I don’t know if I’d confidently say it’s most days. It’s more that I feel like my energy isn’t as reliable as it used to be, if that makes sense.
Over the past few weeks, have you found yourself feeling down, depressed, or losing interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy?

Yeah… I think so. I don’t know that I always would’ve called it “depressed” out loud, because that feels like a big word, but most days lately there’s this kind of heavy, gray feeling that just follows me around.

It’s not only when something bad happens, either. That’s the part that bothers me. I can leave the office, get in the car, go home, and it’s like the mood comes with me. Even if nothing specific is happening in that moment, I’ll just feel kind of hollow, like I’m there but not really connected to anything.

And with things I usually enjoy… I guess I still go through the motions sometimes, but it doesn’t land the same. It’s more like I’m doing things because I know I’m supposed to like them, not because I actually feel much from them. I keep waiting for it to lift, or for something to snap me out of it, but it’s been there enough that I can’t really pretend it’s just a bad day here and there.
Would you say that this low, heavy feeling you've described is present most of the day, nearly every day, even when things around you are fine?

Yeah… I think that’s probably fair. I don’t know if I’d say literally every minute of the day, because there are times I’m distracted or I’m dealing with something at work and I’m not actively thinking, “I feel low right now.” But most days, when I slow down even a little, it’s there.

It’s like this heavy, gray mood just follows me around. I’ll leave the office, get in the car, go home, and it doesn’t really change just because the setting changes or because nothing bad is happening. Sometimes everything around me is technically fine, and I still feel kind of hollow, like I’m just moving through the steps of the day.

So yes, I’d say it’s there most days. Maybe not in this dramatic way where I’m visibly upset all day, but it’s present enough that it feels like the background of everything.
Over the past few weeks, have you had trouble concentrating on things, like work or reading, or found that your mind just doesn’t feel as sharp as it used to?

Yeah, definitely. That’s actually been one of the more frustrating parts, because my job depends on being able to think clearly and move things along.

I used to be able to sit down with sales forecasts or a client deck and kind of just… get into it. Like, I’d review the numbers, figure out the story, clean up the slides, and move on. Now I’ll stare at the same slide over and over, read it five times, and still feel like I’m not absorbing it. Then I start second-guessing every number or every sentence, like, “Is this right? Does this even make sense? Am I missing something obvious?”

And it’s not that the work is suddenly harder, exactly. It’s work I’ve done for years. But my mind feels slower, or less organized. I’ll know I need to make a decision about what to say in a deck or how to frame something for a client, and I just kind of sit there turning it around and around without landing anywhere.

It makes me feel pretty useless sometimes, honestly, because these are things I used to knock out pretty quickly. Now something that should take half an hour can stretch out because I keep rereading, doubting myself, and not really trusting my own thinking.
Have you found that you don’t really get pleasure or satisfaction from things you used to enjoy, even when you make yourself do them?

Yeah… that’s been happening. It’s weird because I still know, in my head, that those are things I like. Or liked. I don’t know how to say it exactly.

Like pickup basketball used to be something I’d look forward to during the week. Even if I was tired from work, once I got there and started playing, I’d feel better. Same with bowling nights — it wasn’t even about bowling that well, it was just being around people, joking around, having something easy to look forward to. Lately I either find a reason not to go, or if I do show up, I’m kind of just… there. I’ll laugh if someone says something funny, but it feels more like I’m reacting because that’s what you do, not because I’m really enjoying myself.

Music festivals too. I used to get excited about the lineup, planning the day, all of that. Now it feels like too much effort, and even if I go, I catch myself standing there thinking, “Why am I not into this?” Like the music is happening, everyone else seems into it, and I’m just watching it from behind glass or something.

And cooking for friends — firing up the smoker, making ribs or brisket or whatever — that used to be a whole thing for me. I liked planning it, checking on it, having people over. Now even that feels flat. I’ll either cancel or keep it really small, and if I do it, it’s like I’m completing a task instead of enjoying it. I hate admitting that, because those were kind of my things.

I’ll laugh if someone says something funny, but it feels more like I’m reacting because that’s what you do, not because I’m really enjoying myself.

Music festivals too. I used to get excited about the lineup, planning the day, all of that. Now it feels like too much effort, and even if I go, I catch myself standing there thinking, “Why am I not into this?” Like the music is happening, everyone else seems into it, and I’m just watching it from behind glass or something.

And cooking for friends — firing up the smoker, making ribs or brisket or whatever — that used to be a whole thing for me. I liked planning it, checking on it, having people over. Now even that feels flat. I’ll either cancel or keep it really small, and if I do it, it’s like I’m completing a task instead of enjoying it. I hate admitting that, because those were kind of my things.

Generalized anxiety disorder (F41.1) and adjustment disorder with depressed mood (F48.0) remain relevant due to overlapping anxiety and stressor-related symptoms, but the duration and persistence of symptoms favor F33.1.
